messages.subject: neg_binomial_log_log
parts:
Hi, I have created neg_binomial_log_log distribution:
https://github.com/randommm/stan/tree/feature/neg_bin

The idea is to help with Negative Binomial regression with log-link the
same way poisson_log_log does. Unit-tests pass.

Is this of interest to (be included in) Stan?


Here follow an example of its usage:

#simple example
y <- rnbinom(100,mu=exp(3),size=5)

fit1 <- stan(model_code="
data {
int y[100];
}
parameters {
real eta;
real<lower=0> phi;
}
model {
y ~ neg_binomial_log(eta, phi);
}
", iter=1e3, data=list(y=y))

print(fit1) #will give appromatelly mean(eta)=3 and mean(phi)=5 =]
# mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
#eta 2.9 0.0 0.0 2.9 2.9 2.9 3.0 3.0 972 1
#phi 8.4 0.1 1.8 5.5 7.1 8.2 9.4 12.3 1154 1
#lp__ 3689.8 0.0 1.0 3687.3 3689.4 3690.1 3690.5 3690.8 563 1




#regression example
x1 <- rnorm(100)
x2 <- rnorm(100,1,2)
y <- rnbinom(100,mu=exp(3-4*x1+2*x2),size=5)

fit2 <- stan(model_code="
data {
vector[100] x1;
vector[100] x2;
int y[100];
}
parameters {
real beta0;
real beta1;
real beta2;
real<lower=0> phi;
}
model {
for (i in 1:100)
y[i] ~ neg_binomial_log(beta0 + beta1*x1[i] + beta2*x2[i], phi);
}
", iter=1e3, data=list(y=y, x1=x1, x2=x2))


fit3 <- stan(model_code="
data {
vector[100] x1;
vector[100] x2;
int y[100];
}
parameters {
real beta0;
real beta1;
real beta2;
real<lower=0> phi;
}
model {
for (i in 1:100)
increment_log_prob(neg_binomial_log_log(y[i], beta0 + beta1*x1[i] +
beta2*x2[i], phi));
}
", iter=1e3, data=list(y=y, x1=x1, x2=x2))

print(fit2)
print(fit3)
#gives similar results (with different __lp of course)
# mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
#beta0 3.0 0.0 0.1 2.8 2.9 3.0 3.0 3.2 626 1
#beta1 -4.1 0.0 0.1 -4.2 -4.1 -4.1 -4.0 -3.9 649 1
#beta2 2.0 0.0 0.0 2.0 2.0 2.0 2.1 2.1 611 1
#phi 4.1 0.0 0.7 2.9 3.6 4.1 4.6 5.5 935 1

------------ Just forwarding a copy of my last post in Github since I
just saw it lost formatting there --------------


Using p as probability of success and r as number of failures until the
experiment is stopped as wikipedia does, we have:

(1) The parametrization in this patch uses
neg_binomial (eta, phi)
with link-function exp(eta)=mu

where p=mu/(mu+phi)
r = phi
and
MEAN = mu
VARIANCE = mu +mu^2/phi

(2) Gelman's book is
neg_binomial (a, b)
where r=a
p=b/(b+1)
and
MEAN = ab
VARIANCE = ab(b+1)

(3) The other parametrization I suggest in the future is:
neg_binomial (mu, phi)
where p=mu/(mu+phi)
r = phi
and
MEAN = mu
VARIANCE = mu +mu^2/phi

(note (3) is for (1) as poisson_log is for poisson_log_log)

(1) is used for GLM, is the parametrization used by Nelder, J.A. &
Wedderburn, R.W.M. (1972). Generalized linear models.
Also used in bayesian inference:
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bayesm/bayesm.pdf (page 71)

(3) seems to be useful when we have a negative binomial response
variable. See
http://doingbayesiandataanalysis.blogspot.com.br/2012/04/negative-binomial-reparameterization.html
It might not be the best practice (if there's best here anyway). I'm not
sure about this because I almost only work with regression this days,
so, this is grey area for me.

(2) I don't know about this one, maybe some people prefer it for uses
like in case (3), or maybe is used as some prior. I haven't read the
whole Bayesian Data Analysis yet and I didn't seem an example there
about it.

This paper uses yet another parametrization in section 4
http://www.johndcook.com/negative_binomial.pdf

About the nomenclature of phi (or r) parameter, I really don't know,
people call it, inverse dispersion, others overdispersion and so on. I
prefer inverse dispersion or something like that 'cause as you see
parametrization (1) and (3), as phi increases, variance decreases. But
in wikipedia parametrization, as r increases, variance increases (this
is because mine set the mean fixed, while Wikipedia's set p fixed) so
maybe that's why overdispersion is somewhat more popular.

Or we could just call it shape since it's same name used for alpha in
the manual (since alpha=r=phi).

About the name of the distribution, whatever is more in the current
standard of Stan, is better for me.

> neg_binomial (a, b)
> where r=a
> p=b/(b+1)
> and
> MEAN = ab
> VARIANCE = ab(b+1)
I guess you mean Bayesian Data analysis? My copies have different equations for mean and variance...

> (2) I don't know about this one, maybe some people prefer it for uses
> like in case (3), or maybe is used as some prior. I haven't read the
> whole Bayesian Data Analysis yet and I didn't seem an example there
> about it.

Parameterization in BDA comes from negative binomial being a mixture of Poisson distributions with rates that follow Gamma(a,b). Thus the parameterization is similar to Student's t, where nu is the degrees of freedom of the Chi^2 scale mixing distribution.

I think it would be nice to use parameterizations in BDA. Maybe they are not always the best parameterizations for each modeling case, but as there is a strong connection between Stan and BDA, it would be nice if they were consistent on parameterizations.

Aki

>
> I think it would be nice to use parameterizations in BDA. Maybe they are not always the best parameterizations for each modeling case, but as there is a strong connection between Stan and BDA, it would be nice if they were consistent on parameterizations.

All of our named distributions (with modifiers) are straight from BDA
other than normal, which uses scale rather than variance because Andrew
said he liked putting priors directly on scale.

For negative binomial, we use

y ~ neg_binomial(alpha,beta)

with parameters:

shape alpha > 0

inverse scale beta > 0,

The mean and variance are:

E[y] : alpha / beta

var[y] : (alpha / beta^2) * (beta + 1)

- Bob
